Quantization stores weights or activations using fewer representable values. This saves memory and data movement. Packed int8 weights take one quarter of the space of fp32 weights, before scales and other metadata. Inference speed also depends on the kernel, its accumulator type, and conversion overhead.
Keep the formats separate:

int8 and int16 store integers. A scale maps them back to the values used by the model.
`fp16` and bfloat16 are 16-bit floating-point formats. Each value has its own exponent.
fp8 names a family of floating-point formats with different ranges and precision.

Post-training quantization uses a trained model. Conversion can happen offline or while loading it; the name describes its relation to training.

metrics for calibration
Calibration chooses the range represented by the quantizer. A wide range includes outliers and spreads the available levels further apart. A narrow range gives finer steps and clips more values. Min/max, percentiles, mean squared reconstruction error, and KL divergence make different choices about that tradeoff. Use representative inputs, then check the model’s task metric. A good histogram match alone does not establish model accuracy. TensorRT’s calibration discussion
KL calibration
Collect an activation histogram, try candidate clipping thresholds, and compare each reference distribution P with a quantized approximation Q expanded onto the same bins:
$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\Vert Q)
= \sum_{j:P_j>0} P_j\log\frac{P_j}{Q_j}.$$
Choose the candidate with the smallest divergence. Both histograms must be normalized. A bin with $P_j>0$ and $Q_j=0$ makes the divergence infinite, so zero-bin handling matters. The comparison is over activation values, even when the network itself produces something other than probabilities. PyTorch’s calibration discussion
fp32 -> fp16
First check the operation’s input, output, and accumulator types. Hardware support varies: CPUs with AVX-512 FP16 can do native half-precision arithmetic. Storing a tensor in fp16 does not determine every intermediate’s precision.

fp32 -> fp16
First check the operation’s input, output, and accumulator types. Hardware support varies: CPUs with AVX-512 FP16 can do native half-precision arithmetic. Storing a tensor in fp16 does not determine every intermediate’s precision.
For IEEE binary16:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{smallest positive normal} &= 2^{-14} \approx 6.10\times10^{-5},\\
\text{smallest positive subnormal} &= 2^{-24} \approx 5.96\times10^{-8},\\
\text{largest finite value} &= (2-2^{-10})2^{15}=65504.
\end{aligned}$$
The normal minimum is often mistaken for the smallest representable value. Subnormals fill part of that gap, with fewer significant bits. Some execution paths flush them to zero. NVIDIA’s half-precision format guide
For a normalization denominator $\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}$, an $\epsilon=10^{-12}$ rounds to zero if converted directly to fp16. A zero variance would then leave a zero denominator. Whether this happens depends on the kernel’s arithmetic: for example, TensorRT normalization defaults to fp32 accumulation. Check the implementation before changing $\epsilon$. Overflow is another failure mode: a reduction can exceed $65504$ even when each input fits. TensorRT accuracy considerations
fp32 -> int8
An affine quantizer has a positive scale $S$, an integer zero point $Z$, and integer limits $q_{\min},q_{\max}$. Quantize and reconstruct with
$$\begin{aligned}
x_q &= \operatorname{clip}\!\left(
  \operatorname{round}(x/S)+Z,\ q_{\min},\ q_{\max}
\right),\\
\hat{x} &= S(x_q-Z).
\end{aligned}$$

fp32 -> int8
An affine quantizer has a positive scale $S$, an integer zero point $Z$, and integer limits $q_{\min},q_{\max}$. Quantize and reconstruct with
$$\begin{aligned}
x_q &= \operatorname{clip}\!\left(
  \operatorname{round}(x/S)+Z,\ q_{\min},\ q_{\max}
\right),\\
\hat{x} &= S(x_q-Z).
\end{aligned}$$
$\hat{x}$ approximates $x$. The zero point makes zero exactly representable when $Z$ lies in the integer range. The integer limits belong to the chosen scheme; signed int8 permits $[-128,127]$, while a symmetric scheme may use $[-127,127]$ with $Z=0$. 1712.05877⁠ (Jacob et al., 2017) 
For example, choose $S=1/127$, $Z=0$, and $[-127,127]$. Then
$$x=0.3
\quad\longrightarrow\quad x_q=38
\quad\longrightarrow\quad \hat{x}=\frac{38}{127}\approx0.29921.$$
Without clipping, nearest rounding gives $|x-\hat{x}|\leq S/2$. A value above $1$ clips to $1$ in this scheme, so that bound no longer applies. A smaller scale improves resolution while reducing the covered range.
For quantized weights and activations, the reconstructed dot product is
$$\sum_i \hat{w}_i\hat{a}_i
= S_wS_a\sum_i(w_{q,i}-Z_w)(a_{q,i}-Z_a).$$
Integer kernels commonly use int32 accumulators for the sum, then rescale the result to the output format. Accumulator width still imposes a limit on the reduction length. The storage type alone does not specify the arithmetic. 1712.05877⁠ (Jacob et al., 2017) 
Per-channel or per-group scales let subsets with different ranges use different step sizes. They add scale metadata, and the kernel must support that layout. PyTorch’s granularity discussion

mxfp4
MXFP4 combines 32 four-bit E2M1 elements with one shared eight-bit E8M0 scale. E2M1 has one sign bit, two exponent bits, and one fraction bit. E8M0 encodes a power-of-two scale, with one reserved NaN encoding. The OCP MX specification defines the block format.
For element $i$,
$$\hat{V}_i=SP_i.$$
The nonnegative E2M1 values are
$$\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,2,3,4,6\}.$$
The scale moves those levels together. A large value in a block can therefore force smaller values onto coarse steps or down to zero. Including the shared scale, storage is
$$\frac{32\cdot4+8}{32}=4.25\ \text{bits per element},$$
before padding and layout overhead.
2310.10537⁠ (Rouhani et al., 2023)  gives an example conversion based on the largest input exponent. For a finite, nonzero block whose resulting scale is representable,
$$\begin{aligned}
e_{\mathrm{shared}}
  &=\left\lfloor\log_2\max_i|V_i|\right\rfloor-2,\\
S&=2^{e_{\mathrm{shared}}},\\
P_i&=Q_{\mathrm{E2M1}}(V_i/S).
\end{aligned}$$
Here $Q_{\mathrm{E2M1}}$ rounds to the element format and clamps finite overflow to $\pm6$. The exponent rule can still clip: a block maximum of $7$ gives $S=1$ and reconstructs as $6$. An all-zero block needs a separate case, such as $S=1$ and all $P_i=0$, because $\log_2 0$ is undefined. The paper presents a conversion recipe; the format allows other recipes.

MX formats apply to both training and inference. A format definition alone gives no guarantee that a particular model trains or retains its accuracy at four bits. The paper evaluates several MX precisions across different workloads.

Stochastic rounding is a separate choice. Between adjacent levels, rounding probabilities can preserve the input in expectation, provided it is in range. Individual samples still lose information, and clipping still introduces bias. 1502.02551⁠ (Gupta et al., 2015) 
quantization time

Post-training dynamic quantization stores quantized weights and selects activation scales from the current inputs at runtime. This adds range-estimation and conversion work.
Post-training static quantization fixes activation scales using representative calibration data before inference. Inputs outside that calibration range can clip. PyTorch’s workflow discussion
Quantization-aware training simulates rounding and clipping in the forward pass while keeping trainable weights in floating point. A straight-through gradient estimator usually substitutes for the derivative of rounding. After training, conversion replaces the simulation with the quantized inference operations. PyTorch’s QAT explanation

methods
bitsandbytes provides quantized operations and model-loading tools. Check the selected format and backend when using it.
GPTQ
2210.17323⁠ (Frantar et al., 2023)  quantizes weights after training. For a layer with weights W and calibration inputs X, its reconstruction objective is
$$\min_{\hat{W}}\ \|WX-\hat{W}X\|_F^2,$$
with $\hat{W}$ constrained to the chosen quantized representation. The calibration inputs reveal which weight errors affect the layer outputs. GPTQ uses approximate second-order information to compensate the remaining weights as it quantizes. Activation precision is a separate choice; GPTQ’s weight quantization alone does not make the whole model integer-only.
floating point
For fp32 and fp16, IEEE 754 binary formats split each scalar into a sign bit, a biased exponent, and a fraction. The fraction is the stored part of the significand.

formattotal bitssign bitsexponent bitsfraction bitsbias Bfp32321823127fp1616151015bfloat1616187127fp8 e5m2815215fp8 e4m381437
Given sign s, stored exponent e, fraction integer f, and fraction width m, a normal value decodes as
x=(-1)^s\left(1+\frac{f}{2^m}\right)2^{e-$B$}.
For subnormals, e=0, the implicit leading bit is zero, and
x_{\mathrm{sub}}=(-1)^$s$\frac{f}{2^m}2^{1-B}.
In fp32 and fp16, an all-ones exponent denotes infinity when the fraction is zero and NaN when it is nonzero. An all-zero exponent and fraction give signed zero. IEEE 754 supports several rounding modes; round-to-nearest, ties-to-even is the default. Overflow handling depends on the rounding mode and conversion operation. CUDA floating-point guide
The FP8 variants need their own special-value rules. E5M2 supports infinities and NaNs. The E4M3 format used here has finite values up to 448 and NaNs, with no infinities; most all-ones exponent encodings remain finite. Transformer Engine’s FP8 primer

decoding 0x40490fdb (fp32)


bits: 0 | 10000000 | 10010010000111111011011
s=0, $e$=128, $f$=\texttt{0x490fdb}=4\,788\,187
$x=\left(1+\frac{4\,788\,187}{2^{23}}\right)2^{128-127}\approx3.14159274$

This is the nearest fp32 value to $\pi$.

bfloat16 keeps the exponent width of fp32, with fewer fraction bits. fp16 spends more of its bits on the fraction and has a smaller exponent range.
